title: Limits
text: Every number on this site comes from a model whose behavioural coefficients are not fitted to observation. The physics is real; the trajectory is structural, not predictive.

title: Limits
text:
1. The dominant coefficients are unfitted
Morris screening puts p_cap (annual purchase hazard ceiling) and b0 (baseline propensity) at the top of every output. Neither is a measured quantity. Until they are calibrated against AC ownership by income band, room-AC sales trends and licensee summer load growth, the level of the trajectory is a choice, not a finding. The shape — who adopts first, where waste heat concentrates, how fabric and income interact — is far more robust than the level.

title: Limits
section: 2. ΔT is a uniform city-mean increment
text:
2. ΔT is a uniform city-mean increment
The feedback uses a scalar transfer coefficient applied equally to every hour and every ward. Real AC waste heat concentrates at night and in dense areas: published coupled simulations find little daytime effect and roughly 0.6–1.5 °C of night-time warming where cooling is widespread. This model therefore understates night warming in adopting wards and overstates daytime warming everywhere. Replacing \(k\) with SUEWS or PALM-4U per local climate zone is the single largest physics upgrade available.

title: Limits
text:
3. Placeholder building parameters
Energy use intensities, appliance stocks, U-values, air change rates, thermal capacitance and roof solar gains are all plausible values chosen by hand. No Indian archetype library is used. The model was tuned once against city peak electricity (~4,000 MW across the four licensees) and left there; further tuning without measured data would be fitting noise.

title: Limits
text:
4. Input data limits
Heights carry 1.5–9 m error, propagating into floor counts, floor area, capacitance and household counts. Typology is roughly 35% evidence-supported; the remainder comes from a size-and-height heuristic. The slum layer is 2016 and sets archetype, thermal properties and income band simultaneously, so its vintage propagates into all three — Mumbai’s informal stock has changed since, particularly where redevelopment has occurred. The income proxy is land value.

title: Limits
text:
5. Physics simplifications

COP fixed at 3.0. Real COP degrades as ambient temperature rises, so cooling energy and waste heat are understated exactly when they matter most.
All condenser heat treated as sensible. Commercial cooling towers reject mostly latent heat; in a coastal, humid city that distinction changes the surface energy balance.
Vehicle heat rests on one invented number — city-wide daily vehicle-kilometres — yet contributes a large share of total Qf. It is the least constrained term in the model.
Solar gain is a flat clear-sky proxy with no shading, orientation or sky view factor.

title: Limits
text:
6. Structural omissions

The stock is frozen to 2040: no redevelopment, no new construction, no population growth. Over fifteen years Mumbai’s redevelopment pipeline probably changes cooling demand more than adoption behaviour does.
No daytime population redistribution. Metabolic heat sits at people’s homes all day, understating Qf in BKC, Nariman Point and Lower Parel during working hours and overstating it in the suburbs.
No tenure split. Renters cannot install, landlords do not pay bills; the split-incentive problem is large in Mumbai’s rental and chawl stock.
No tariff slabs. Maharashtra residential tariffs telescope steeply, so crossing a slab sharply raises marginal cost. Electricity price does not enter the decision at all.
No replacement cycle. Units are bought and never retired, so efficiency standards cannot be tested.
Commercial and industrial cooling is exogenous — a fixed fraction per archetype — despite being 43% of modelled energy.

title: Limits
text:
7. What is not a limitation
Stochastic uncertainty. With 3.2 million households, seed variance in 2040 penetration is under 0.1 percentage points. Presenting replicate ensembles as uncertainty quantification would be misleading; the uncertainty is in the coefficients.

title: Results
text:
City-scale magnitude agrees. The diurnal shape does not, and that is the point: the benchmark’s profile is derived from US utility load curves and peaks mid-afternoon, while this model — built from Indian appliance schedules and evening-weighted residential demand — peaks at 18:00.
Composition of the 2026 total over built cells: buildings dominate, road traffic contributes a large and poorly constrained share, human metabolism about 4 W/m².

Informal dwellings run 1.6 °C hotter on average and 4.0 °C hotter at peak than tower flats, carry 65% more discomfort degree-hours, and operate cooling at 64% of the rate. Two mechanisms produce that: an uninsulated low roof over a small dwelling (45 W/m² roof gain, 3 air changes per hour) and a household that cannot afford to run a machine it may not own.
The outdoor heat those households are exposed to is produced largely by other people’s air conditioners. That asymmetry — private benefit, shared cost — is the result the model exists to quantify.

Two readings, both worth stating:
The answer is set by the two parameters with no empirical anchor. p_cap (the annual purchase hazard ceiling) and b0 (baseline propensity) dominate every output. They are calibration knobs, not measured quantities. That is what makes this a prototype, and it says exactly where to spend effort next.

title: Results
text:
5. On ensembles
Stochastic replicates are not this model’s uncertainty. Across seeds, 2040 penetration varies by under 0.1 percentage points: with 3.2 million households, binomial noise averages out completely. The uncertainty lives in the coefficients, which is why screening and calibration matter here and ensembles do not.

title: Method
text:
1. Stock
Floors are ceil(height / storey height) with storey height set per use class, clipped to [1, 90]. Floor area is footprint × floors. Wards are joined by centroid, with a 100 m snap for near-boundary cases; 92,693 buildings fall outside Greater Mumbai altogether (Thane, Mira-Bhayandar, Navi Mumbai) and are dropped.

title: Method
text:
2. Population and income
Ward population (MCGM mid-2023) is distributed across residential floor area within each ward, then divided by archetype occupancy to give households. Income band is a quartile of the ward’s ready-reckoner rate, with slum-flagged buildings pinned to the lowest band — land value is a poor income proxy precisely where informal settlements sit inside expensive wards.

title: Method
text:
3. Loads and waste heat
\[
P_\text{base}(t) = \sum_\text{appliances} (\text{ownership} \times \text{rated power}) \times \sigma(t)
\]
\[
UA = U A_\text{env} + 0.33\, n_\text{ACH} V
\]
\[
Q_\text{cool}(t) = \big[UA \max(0, T_\text{out} - T_\text{set}) + Q_\text{sol} + Q_\text{int}\big] \times \text{occupancy} \times \text{runtime}
\]
\[
Q_f(t) = P_\text{base}(t) + Q_\text{cool}(t) + \frac{Q_\text{cool}(t)}{\text{COP}} \equiv P_\text{base} + Q_\text{cool}\left(1 + \tfrac{1}{\text{COP}}\right)
\]
Base electricity becomes indoor heat and is simultaneously an internal gain to the cooling load, so the two terms are physically coupled. Splitting base from cooling is what allows adoption to change anything.
Two non-building terms are added at the grid stage: human metabolism (70 W asleep, 140 W awake, following the residential occupancy schedule, placed at people’s homes) and road traffic (city-wide daily vehicle-kilometres distributed across cells by class-weighted OSM road length, shaped by a twin-peak traffic profile).

title: Method
text:
4. Indoor temperature (1R1C)
Adoption is driven by discomfort, and discomfort is felt indoors. A single-capacitance model per building gives free-running indoor air temperature:
\[
C \frac{dT_\text{in}}{dt} = UA_\text{eff}\,(T_\text{out} - T_\text{in}) + Q_\text{sol} + Q_\text{int}
\]
with \(C\) = capacitance per m² × floor area, and \(UA_\text{eff}\) built from fabric plus open-window ventilation — not the closed-window ACH used for cooling load — boosted at night when outdoor air is cooler. Solar gain includes a roof term that matters only for low-rise dwellings, where roof area per dwelling is large. Integrated hourly over a repeating typical day with a five-day spin-up.
This is what makes archetypes differ. Without it, every household in the city experiences the same stimulus and the building stock does no work.

title: Method
text:
5. Feedback
\[
\Delta T(t+1) = k \big[\overline{Q_f}(t) - \overline{Q_f}(\text{baseline})\big]
\]
\(\Delta T\) raises the next year’s outdoor temperature series, which raises both cooling demand and indoor discomfort. \(k\) is a transfer coefficient standing in for a surface energy balance model; it is the largest physics assumption in the project and is swept explicitly. See Limits.

section: Phase A — calibration (changes the model’s status)
text:
Phase A — calibration (changes the model’s status)
Morris says p_cap and b0 dominate; both are pure knobs. Fit them, leave the rest.

History matching to rule out implausible coefficient space, using two anchors: current AC ownership by income band, and the observed licensee summer load trend.
ABC for credible intervals on the surviving space.
Report trajectories as bands over coefficient uncertainty, not over seeds.

section: Phase B — replace the uniform ΔT
text:
Phase B — replace the uniform ΔT
SUEWS through UMEP, one run per LCZ class, forced by MCGM AWS. Gives night-vs-day and dense-vs-sparse differentiation, which is where the AC feedback literature finds its signal. The MMR LCZ map already exists.

section: Phase C — behavioural additions, cheapest first
text:
Phase C — behavioural additions, cheapest first

Tariff slabs — free from MERC orders, affects adoption and runtime.
Tenure — one binary attribute from Census ward ownership share; split incentives.
Replacement cycle — lets efficiency standards be tested at all.
Commercial cooling inside the ABM — currently exogenous, 43% of energy.

Phase D — structural

Redevelopment pipeline: chawls → towers changes archetype mix over 15 years.
Daytime population from Time Use Survey schedules.
Extend to MMR once ward-equivalent population exists for Thane and Navi Mumbai (92,693 buildings already extracted, saved in data/interim/buildings_out_of_scope.parquet).

Traps already hit

Multi-line Python pasted into bash: always cat > file <<'PYEOF' or python - <<'PYEOF'.
pip install into conda base broke NumPy compatibility across pandas/pyarrow/numba. The project has its own env now; NumPy pinned <2.
python -m http.server ignores Range requests, so PMTiles fails silently. Use RangeHTTPServer; GitHub Pages handles ranges correctly.
Tippecanoe drops up to 97% of features when tiles exceed 500 KB. Use --no-feature-limit --no-tile-size-limit, drop empty cells, round to integers.
MCGM ward codes arrive as F/ S, G /N with stray spaces — normalise before joining.
Slum sjoin produced 860 duplicate rows from overlapping polygons — dissolve first.
Population allocation fails silently on ward-code mismatch; 02 now raises below 90%.
SALib 1.6 requires NumPy ≥2 — pin SALib <1.6.

title: Interactive map
text:
Hourly anthropogenic heat on a 100 m grid, for four snapshot years of the adoption model. Drag the year slider to watch waste heat grow as households buy air conditioners; drag the hour slider to see the evening peak build. Click any cell for its value across all four years.

Open the map full screen
Reading it. The island city and the eastern suburbs carry the highest values; SGNP, Aarey and the creeks are empty because no buildings sit there. Cell-level variance is real rather than noise — a 100 m cell holding one tower differs sharply from its neighbour holding three chawls — but at this resolution the picture is grainier than a published Qf atlas would normally be shown.

title: Data
text:
The income proxy
The eASR portal disallows automated access, so ward-level rates were derived from published compilations of the same official schedule: 125 revenue-village localities, manually mapped to wards with a confidence flag, then taken as a median per ward. The spread is 7.3× from M/East (₹53,970/m²) to A ward (₹3,92,624/m²), which is enough to define four meaningful income bands.
It remains land value, not income. Its worst failure — informal settlements inside expensive wards, such as Dharavi in G/North or Behrampada in H/East — is handled by pinning slum-flagged buildings to the lowest band regardless of rate.

title: Data
text:
The weather record
The daily series splices two sources, visible in the decimal precision: 1951–2019 is a gridded product (April–May median Tmax ≈ 35.9 °C, daily range ≈ 12 °C), 2020–2024 is station data (34.5 °C, range ≈ 8.5 °C). The gridded era is inland-biased and would overstate cooling demand, so only the station era is used. A typical pre-monsoon day is taken as the April–May median and expanded to 24 hours with a Parton–Logan curve.
One consequence: a single series means no urban heat island gradient. Every ward receives identical forcing, and the only spatial variation in indoor temperature comes from building fabric.

title: Anthropogenic heat and air-conditioner adoption in Greater Mumbai
text:
Every air conditioner moves heat from inside a building to the street. As Mumbai’s households buy them, the city’s waste heat rises — and the households least able to afford cooling live in the dwellings that get hottest.
This project quantifies both halves of that sentence for all 580,890 buildings inside the 24 BMC wards.

title: Anthropogenic heat and air-conditioner adoption in Greater Mumbai
text:
What this is
Two models, coupled.
A bottom-up urban building energy model. Building footprints and heights become a stock of typed archetypes. Each carries an appliance load and a cooling load driven by outdoor temperature, and each rejects waste heat to the street: base electricity roughly one-to-one, plus condenser heat of Qcool(1 + 1/COP). Human metabolism and road traffic are added, and the total is aggregated to a 100 m grid at hourly resolution.
An agent-based model of who buys an air conditioner. Households are agents. Each year, every household without an AC decides whether to buy one, based on what it can afford, how hot its own dwelling gets, and how many of its neighbours already have one. Those that own one choose a setpoint and how long to run it. The resulting waste heat raises the city’s temperature, which raises next year’s discomfort — the loop that makes this an ABM rather than a projection.

title: Anthropogenic heat and air-conditioner adoption in Greater Mumbai
text:
What it shows
The city-scale magnitude checks out. Qf over built cells comes to 20.58 W/m² against 23.5 W/m² from the published extrapolation for Mumbai, but peaks at 18:00 rather than 16:00. That two-hour gap is the substantive result: the benchmark’s diurnal shape comes from US utility load curves, while Indian residential demand peaks in the evening.
Adoption roughly triples by 2040, adding 3.2 W/m² of waste heat and 452 MW of peak demand, with no population growth or new construction in the model.
Thermal inequality is measurable and it runs the wrong way. Informal dwellings sit 1.6 °C hotter on average and 4.0 °C hotter at peak than tower flats, carry 65% more discomfort degree-hours, and run cooling at 64% of the rate. The heat they are exposed to outdoors is produced largely by other people’s machines.
The two mechanisms are separable. Sensitivity screening puts affordability and the baseline purchase rate at the top and indoor discomfort near the bottom for adoption, while discomfort produces the largest spread across the stock. Income and price decide who adopts; building fabric decides who suffers while not adopting.

This is an uncalibrated prototype. The building physics and the agent logic are real; the behavioural coefficients are not fitted to observation, and the two that dominate the result have no empirical anchor. Treat trajectories as structural, not predictive. See Limits.

title: Anthropogenic heat and air-conditioner adoption in Greater Mumbai
text:
Built in a day
The whole pipeline — data assembly, energy model, thermal model, ABM, sensitivity screening, web map — was built in a single session on 19 September 2026, then paused for documentation. Reproduce has the commands.

title: The agent-based model
text:
A spreadsheet can multiply an assumed penetration rate by a cooling load. Three things here need agents:
Heterogeneity that interacts with the physics. The dwelling that gets hottest belongs to the household least able to buy cooling. That correlation determines the aggregate, and it cannot be recovered from city means.
Peer effects. Adoption spreads through neighbourhoods. The share of nearby households already owning an AC enters each decision, so adoption compounds spatially instead of rising uniformly.
A feedback loop. Waste heat raises outdoor temperature, which raises indoor temperature, which raises discomfort, which raises adoption. The loop only exists if the agents re-read their environment each year.

title: The agent-based model
text:
Agents
One household cohort per residential building: an integer count of households, of which an integer count own an air conditioner. That makes 3.2 million household agents cost two integer arrays rather than three million Python objects.







attribute
source




households

ready-reckoner quartile, slums pinned to the lowest

typology + floor count + slum flag

title: The agent-based model
text:
The decision
Each year, every household without an AC draws against
\[
u = \beta_0 + \beta_a (\text{afford} - 1) + \beta_d \left(\frac{\text{discomfort}_i}{\text{discomfort}_\text{ref}} - 1\right) + \beta_p\, \text{peer}_i
\]
\[
p_i = \frac{p_\text{cap}}{1 + e^{-u}}
\]

afford rises with real income growth against a falling real AC price, scaled down at low income bands (the same price is a larger barrier further down the distribution).
discomforti is that agent’s own indoor degree-hours above the comfort threshold, including any warming the city has caused itself.
peeri is the share of households owning an AC within the agent’s neighbourhood, computed on a 500 m grid with 3×3 smoothing rather than a radius query — the calculation repeats every simulated year over 580,890 buildings.

Adoption is a binomial draw on the non-owning households, so penetration is an output. Nothing forces the trajectory toward a target.

title: The agent-based model
text:
Operation
Ownership is a weak proxy for heat output: a household cooling one room for two hours a night and one cooling a whole flat for ten differ fourfold. Two behavioural variables close that gap.
Setpoint falls with income band (27 °C at the bottom, 24 °C at the top). Runtime is logistic in mean indoor exceedance above the setpoint, damped by a bill sensitivity that is lower for poorer households. Both are read back by the load model.

The city-wide mean runtime is where the inequality shows up in aggregate: it dropped from 0.74 to 0.60 the moment 284,216 buildings were reclassified as informal, because those households sit in the highest-setpoint, most bill-sensitive group. Operation behaviour, not ownership, did that.

title: The agent-based model
text:
What the model is not
It has no replacement cycle (units are bought, never retired), no explicit tariff slabs, no tenure split between owners and renters, and no change in the building stock — no redevelopment, no new construction, no population growth. Commercial and industrial cooling is a fixed fraction per archetype and sits outside the ABM entirely, despite being 43% of modelled energy.
